cases.answer: Split before preprocessing. Fit the scaler on training rows only, then transform training and test rows with that fitted scaler; otherwise test features leak into evaluation and make it optimistic.
Held-out rows must never determine scaling statistics. Split first, fit the scaler to the training rows, and apply that same scaler to both sets.
required_corrections: Held-out preprocessing statistics can make the test score optimistic.

cases.answer: There is no leakage because scaling uses features rather than test labels. Scaling all rows is fine.
required_corrections: Test features can leak through fitted preprocessing statistics; split before fitting.

cases.answer: Accuracy is dominated by legitimate email, so an all-negative filter gets 98% while finding no spam. Precision is true spam among flagged messages; recall is found spam among all actual spam.
The filter is excellent because 98% accuracy means it catches 98% of spam.
required_corrections: Overall accuracy does not show spam recall in an imbalanced set.

cases.answer: In a confusion matrix, an all-negative filter has zero true positives and misses every actual spam. Spam precision is TP / (TP + FP), while spam recall is TP / (TP + FN), so 98% accuracy is only the majority-class baseline.

Bagging fits trees independently on bootstrap samples drawn with replacement and averages their predictions. Boosting fits each new tree to improve the current ensemble's errors, then adds that stage's scaled contribution to the ensemble.
Both methods combine many models, so they always do the same thing.
required_corrections: Bagging fits independent bootstrap trees and aggregates them, whereas boosting adds sequential stages that improve the current ensemble.

cases.answer: Backpropagation applies the chain rule from the loss backward to compute each parameter gradient. An optimiser then uses those gradients to update weights and reduce loss.

Use batch inference for the overnight catalogue because a scheduled high-throughput job can score all items and save results. Use online inference for the waiting shopper because the prediction needs low latency and serving capacity when requests arrive.

Falling training loss while validation loss rises is overfitting: additional stages fit training details but hurt generalisation. Choose the rounds at minimum validation loss, or use early stopping with patience; shallow trees or regularisation can slow complexity growth.
Each random-forest tree trains on rows sampled with replacement. At every split it considers a random subset of features; for regression, the forest averages the trees' predictions.

Generalisation is performance on unseen rentals from the intended population. Small training error but much larger held-out error suggests overfitting. Estimate new-rental performance on data held out from both fitting and tuning, using a split that reflects deployment.

Immediately compare input distributions or missing-value rates with a reference baseline; a shift signals investigation, not proof that accuracy fell. When outcomes arrive, match them to the original predictions and compare a relevant metric such as return recall with its baseline over a comparable window.
Persist preprocessing with the trained model and apply the same fitted transformations at inference. Version code, features and data assumptions so a prediction can be reproduced.
If all trees make the same errors, averaging barely helps. Resampling and random feature choices create different trees, allowing averaging to cancel some individual errors.
